Describe anything in English this month

issue.preview_text: Plus a 6-day adjectives course, 30+ phrases for Mexico and practice tips for quiet learners.

body.text: Hi [First name], September on the blog was all about describing things. Six guides took English adjectives apart from every angle, so we turned them into a short email course. Here are the reads worth your time.

body.section: Lead: 80+ most common adjectives in English
body.text: The adjectives you’ll reach for most, grouped so they’re easy to learn. It also shows which adjectives count as “short” (one syllable, or two syllables ending in -y) and which count as “long”, which decides how you compare things.
Prefer one small step a day? Join the 6-day adjectives course: one lesson and one practice task each morning.

body.section: Also worth your time: 120+ countries and nationalities in English
body.text: For most countries you can guess the nationality by adding -an or -ian (Italy, Italian). And nationalities always take a capital letter.

body.section: Also worth your time: Why is English spelling so tricky?
body.text: English spelling was set down in layers, and then the sounds kept moving. The Great Vowel Shift (15th to 18th centuries) changed how vowels sounded but not how they were written, and the k and gh in “knight” were once pronounced too.

body.section: Also worth your time: 30+ common Spanish phrases for your trip to Mexico
body.text: Greet people with buenos días when you walk into a shop, and ask “¿Pica mucho?” before you order something spicy.

body.section: New and worth a look: Dear Duolingo on practising as an introvert
body.text: Six tips (plus a bonus) for building your skills at your own pace, from writing first to talking to yourself and shadowing audio.
How much do you know about Italian?
Hit reply and tell us the English word you always misspell. [Name]

lessons.subject: Day 1: the adjective families
lessons.idea: Adjectives do more than describe. Some point (this, that), some show ownership (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), some ask questions (which, what, whose). Today: meet the families so the rest of the week has a map. This course covers the most common adjectives, descriptive ones, word order, how strong an adjective can get, and this/that/these/those.
lessons.task: Write one sentence that uses a describing adjective, a possessive one and a pointing one.

lessons.subject: Day 2: the 80 you’ll use most
lessons.idea: A short list does most of the work. Learn the common adjectives in groups, and notice which are short (one syllable, or two ending in -y) and which are long: that decides how you compare them.
lessons.task: Pick five adjectives from the list and sort them into short and long.

lessons.subject: Day 3: adjectives that never change
lessons.idea: In English, a descriptive adjective keeps the same form for one thing or many, and for any gender. One cold drink, two cold drinks.
lessons.task: Describe three things in your room, then the same things in the plural, and check that the adjective stayed the same.

lessons.subject: Day 4: which adjective goes first?
lessons.idea: Stacked adjectives follow an order: opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material, purpose. That’s why it’s “a delicious square cake”, not “a square delicious cake”.
lessons.task: Describe your favourite mug with three adjectives in the right order.

lessons.subject: Day 5: a little cold or very married?
lessons.idea: Most adjectives come in degrees: water can be a little cold or very cold. Some don’t: you can’t be a little married. Knowing which is which keeps “very” where it belongs.
lessons.task: Write two sentences with “very” that work, and one that doesn’t, and explain why.

lessons.subject: Day 6: this, that, these, those
lessons.idea: Four small words point at things: near or far, one or many. Use them to say exactly which thing you mean. That’s the course: reply and tell us which day helped most.
lessons.task: Point at four objects around you and name each with the right word.
